Halitosis is the formal, medical word for bad breath — an unpleasant or offensive odour that comes from a person's mouth when they breathe or speak.
What it means in plain terms

When someone's breath smells bad — whether mildly unpleasant or strongly foul — that condition is called halitosis. It is not a disease on its own, but rather a symptom or condition that can have various causes. Doctors, dentists, and medical writers use this word instead of the everyday phrase "bad breath" because it sounds more precise and clinical.

Understanding the causes helps you fully grasp what the word refers to:

  • Poor dental hygiene — Not brushing or flossing properly leaves food particles in your mouth. Bacteria break down these particles and release foul-smelling gases, which is the most common reason.
  • Food and drink — Certain foods like garlic, onions, and strong spices, as well as coffee and alcohol, temporarily cause halitosis because their odour-producing compounds enter your bloodstream and are exhaled through your lungs.
  • Dry mouth (xerostomia) — Saliva helps clean the mouth. When your mouth is dry (from dehydration, sleeping with your mouth open, or certain medications), bacteria multiply faster, worsening the smell.
  • Gum disease (periodontitis) — Infected or inflamed gums produce a distinctly bad odour.
  • Tooth decay or cavities — Rotting teeth harbour bacteria that smell strongly.
  • Tongue coating — A white or yellow layer on the back of the tongue is a dense colony of bacteria and is one of the leading causes.
  • Medical conditions — Conditions like acid reflux, sinusitis, tonsil infections, diabetes (which can cause a fruity or acetone-like breath smell), kidney failure, or liver problems can all produce characteristic types of halitosis.
  • Smoking and tobacco — These leave a persistent chemical smell in the mouth and lungs, and also damage gum tissue, making halitosis worse over time.

This is an important distinction:

  • Temporary halitosis is the kind almost everyone experiences at some point — morning breath (when saliva flow drops during sleep and bacteria thrive), or the lingering smell after eating garlic. This is normal and resolves on its own or with brushing and hydration.
  • Chronic halitosis is persistent bad breath that keeps returning no matter how much someone brushes their teeth. This is the form that is considered a genuine medical concern and usually has an underlying cause that needs to be addressed by a dentist or doctor.

You will mostly encounter halitosis in:

  • Medical and dental contexts — when a dentist records a patient's condition or a doctor documents a symptom.
  • Health articles and journalism — writers use it to sound authoritative and precise.
  • Product marketing — mouthwash, toothpaste, and chewing gum brands sometimes use the word in their advertising to describe what their product "treats" or "prevents," lending a clinical, trustworthy tone.

In everyday conversation, people almost always say "bad breath" instead of halitosis. Saying "he has halitosis" in casual speech would sound overly formal or even a little humorous — the kind of phrasing you might hear in an old advertisement.

Halitosis is very common. Studies suggest that roughly one in four people experience it regularly. It can affect a person's self-confidence and social interactions significantly, causing embarrassment or anxiety in conversations. Beyond the social impact, chronic halitosis is often a signal that something in the body — most commonly the mouth — needs attention. This is why dentists take it seriously as a diagnostic indicator.

Treatment depends entirely on the cause:

  • Better oral hygiene (brushing twice daily, flossing, cleaning the tongue) addresses the most common cause.
  • Staying well-hydrated helps prevent dry mouth.
  • Regular dental check-ups catch gum disease and decay early.
  • If the cause is a medical condition (like acid reflux or diabetes), treating that condition usually resolves the halitosis.
  • Mouthwashes and breath fresheners mask the smell temporarily but do not cure the underlying problem.

Halitosis = bad breath, specifically the unpleasant odour coming from the mouth. It ranges from mild and temporary (like morning breath) to chronic and socially distressing (when caused by gum disease, decay, or a medical condition). The word is clinical in register, meaning it is at home in medical, dental, and formal written contexts, but in everyday speech, "bad breath" is the natural equivalent.
